responseSet.title: Adjustment to Future Realities
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Adjustment to Future Realities

Harry Is ‘Mixed Up’

147th Interview: Harry opened his notebook to an account of some recent dreams and read aloud to Dr. T. One of the dreams was about a girl. That reminded Harry that, when he saw boys and girls going out together, he would decide that he himself wouldn't go out with a girl unless she was the motherly type.

Harry: I'm mixed up about this, but I have an idea that you want me to be mixed up.

Dr. T: I want you to be …. Why should you think so?

Harry: I don't know exactly. Generally, though, I think you believe that it's good for people to be uncertain in life. But it could be that I'm wrong. Maybe you really want me to be happy after all.

Dr. T: Why not? Why shouldn't you be happy?

Harry: I think I'll go home and decide not to be mixed up and unhappy any more.

Dr. T: A good idea. But, first of all, tell me this: Why is it that you think about going home and being happy simply because I don't object to your being happy?

Harry: Well, I suppose it's because I think I should agree when somebody tells me something. I guess I don't think too much about what I want myself. My mother always tells me: “Harry, you must go along with people. You must agree with what they say.”

responseSet.title: Working Through to Current Realities
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Working Through to Current Realities

“Will You Adopt Me?”

90th Interview: The interview took place two days after Mrs. Baker had complained to the agency that Harry was refusing to go to school, was spending much of the day in bed, and that his behavior in general had become “impossible.” Interrupting his mother's telephone conversation with Dr. T, Harry had said he could see no value in their conversation, even though he had no objection to his mother discussing him with his therapist.

Harry began the interview by remarking that he understood he was required by law to attend school until he was 16. He would probably return to school, although he would rather work in an office. He did not want to study. He wanted to be independent.

Although his mother was very good to him and he liked staying with her, he felt that they would be better off if they were separated. He “just didn't know how” to get along with her. He had been staying home because he felt better lying in bed than doing anything else. On the whole, though, he was unhappy; he felt that nobody loved him.

Harry did not, as a rule, enjoy being depressed, he said, but he remembered how much better he had once felt after “crying something out.” One solution might be for the therapist to get Harry so depressed that he would cry for a week. In that way, he could solve all his problems and be happy evermore.

The boy had his doubts about that solution, though.

122

responseSet.title: Appendix A: The Early Curriculum
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Appendix A: The Early Curriculum

PT Level A

Required Courses

PT 1M Maturation in Psychoanalysis Two Semesters
The modern psychoanalytic theory of maturation. How maturational needs unfold in psychoanalysis.
PT 2 Psychopathology Two Semesters
FIRST SEMESTER: Differential diagnosis based on presenting symptoms, defense patterns and psychic structure.
SECOND SEMESTER: Sections on pathology in childhood, adolescence, adults, families and groups.
PT 3 Basic Psychoanalytic Theory Two Semesters
FIRST SEMESTER: Intensive study of Freud's basic theoretical concepts and method of therapy. Readings in Freud.
SECOND SEMESTER: Modern psychoanalytic theory based on Freud's concepts of resistance. Other readings.
PT 4a Modern Psychoanalytic Theory of Treatment and Supervision One Semester
Distinguished Lecture Series. The course deals with the development of ideas on how to become a mature personality and a mature analyst.
PT 4b Theory of Technique (Elective) One Semester
Modern psychoanalytic technique. Patterns of communication and resistance emerging in beginning, middle, and end phase of treatment.
PT 5 Medical Knowledge for Psychoanalysts Two Semesters

5A. Neuroanatomy and Physiology

Historical and philosophical aspects of the mind, the evolution of the state of consciousness. Embryology of the central nervous system presented and correlated with adult structure. The human brain is used to teach gross and microscopic structure. These exercises permit the student to integrate neuroanatomical knowledge with rational and emotional behavior. The course explores the relationship between functions of the mind, both rational and emotional, and modern psychoanalytic theory.

5B. The Chemistry and Biology of the Human Sexual and Reproductive Functions

The behavioral and structural aspects of human sexual behavior. Details of the embryology of the genital organs related to adult function. Endocrine control of maturation and details of the reproductive process will be illustrated.

Facilitating Ego Maturation

“Are You Godlike or Are You Normal?”

From an Interview with Harry's Mother: “Up and down” was the way Mrs. Baker characterized Harry's behavior.

Her therapist had the impression that the boy's mother had little comprehension of his difficulties. She seemed to expect Harry to behave as if he did not have any. She preached to him a great deal, and apparently hoped to influence him by “right thinking.”

56th Interview: A dream of being in a subway station with a friend was related by Harry as soon as he arrived. As the two of them were crossing some tracks, they saw six persons approaching them from a tunnel. They first appeared to be girls, but on closer inspection turned out to be three girls and three boys—“rough and tough” figures. Harry and his friend left the station and then he woke up.

With the dream, the youngster associated two memories of being in a car with his grandfather and mother. In the first, he punched her in the nose for refusing him something he wanted. Then, Harry said, he could see that his mother regretted the incident. The second memory was of a car door being slammed so hard on his thumb that he feared part of it had come off.

[Harry regarded his grandfather as a preeminently virtuous person

responseSet.title: After Sixteen Years of Experimentation: The Current Program
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

After Sixteen Years of Experimentation: The Current Program

The current program is based on a decade of experience, decisions made at the Bahamas Conference on Curriculum, and subsequent trials with these ideas. It includes four years of maturation theory, a history sequence consisting of three years of psychonalytic history and one year of psychoanalytic research; four years of basic theoretical concepts; and a clinical studies sequence including two years of mental hospital placement working with three or more psychotic patients and three or more years of supervised psychoanalytic practice in the Center's Referral Service, during which a final project is prepared.

In the early years the tendency of new faculty was to imitate the style of their own teachers, the senior faculty. Recently we have seen a tendency of instructors to develop teaching styles reflective of their own personalities. The overall goal remains the same: to experiment with emotional education.

The faculty of the Center consists of senior analysts who have contributed to scholarship and treatment since the fifties and sixties. Faculty additions have been made predominately from gifted graduates. The program itself was prepared by Meadow after consultation with senior faculty. Modifications take place as faculty members study the effectiveness of readings.

In the following segment, I have included the courses, by title, the current reference lists, and the ideas of the current faculty on how and why they teach the way they do. I have included faculty publications available in the journal, Modern Psychoanalysis. It is my hope that this review of a modern training program will provide the impetus for further investigations of what makes good training and how people learn to be psychoanalysts.

responseSet.title: Appendix B: Training in Modern Group Analysis
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Appendix B: Training in Modern Group Analysis

In 1986, the Center added a separate program in group analysis, removing group training to this later phase. However, the history of the development of group analysis is included in the regular program. The training program in group analysis includes courses in the theory, practice, and technique of modern group analysis; the management of group-destructive resistances; the manifestations of the major psychoanalytic concepts as they operate in and are modified by the group setting; the identification and resolution of individual, subgroup, and group resistances; continuous group case seminars; and group supervision.

Since there is no time limit for completion of courses, candidates proceed at their own pace. Each semester, group supervision of private therapy groups is available. Candidates should have had, or be currently involved in, an approved psychoanalytic therapy group for at least 120 hours.

Modern analytic group psychotherpay aims at eliciting and resolving the resistances of individual members, subgroups, and finally, of the group as a whole. Resistances are viewed as an expression of the individual's characteristic modes of functioning which emerged in the adaptation to the pressures and stresses of his or her very first group—the family. Resistance is thus identified with survival. A second function associated with resistance is that of providing significant information about the patient's life history: the role the patient adopts in the group reflects the behavioral patterns developed in the face of psychological exigencies in the family.

responseSet.title: The Maturation Sequence
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Maturation Sequence

The Maturation Process from Conception through the First Year of Life (PT 101)

This course was developed by Ethel Goldwater Clevans as the best introduction to the treatment of preverbal disorders. Clevans emphasized the relieving. She agreed with Winnicott and Spotnitz that at this stage of development there is only now; whatever remains from the past is experienced as having its total reality in the present. This is how Winnicott described psychotic transference: the feelings about the self and the caretakers are not remembered—the past is the present: not “you are like my mother,” but “you are my mother.”3

It is currently taught every other semester by Don Shapiro and one semester in alternate years by Dorothy Gloster and Faye Miller, all Center graduates. Shapiro is the author of Modern psychoanalytic research and A portrait of Ethel Clevans. Shapiro, in his discussion of this course, points out that psychoanalysis has only gradually extended its perspective to include infancy and prenatal growth, and that we should expect to find intense difficulty in communicating meaningfully within this realm.

Shapiro refers to this developmental period as one concerned with the fundamental issues of life and death. He poses nine questions designed to focus on some of the difficulties of this period of growth. Addressing the class, he asks:

Is this a group of people you would like to know?

Is everyone feeling passionate, loving involvement here?

Are we people you would like to raise a child with?

3All quotes refer to an attached reading list for the course under discussion.235

responseSet.title: Introduction to the Case of Harry
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Introduction to the Case of Harry

The name “Harry Baker” was selected to preserve the anonymity of the subject of this case presentation. Its publication was sanctioned by the boy and his mother on the understanding that their true identities would not be divulged. The external circumstances are suitably disguised, but Harry's thoughts and feelings, his problems and progress, actions and aspirations are recorded as he communicated them in the course of his treatment.

Harry's treatment was conducted in the 1950s, a period when a growing number of seriously disturbed children were coming to the attention of child guidance agencies (Feldman, 1978). Under the direction of the principal author, who served as consultant psychiatrist to one of these agencies, the Jewish Board of Guardians, New York City, a research project was established at the Bronx office of the JBG to investigate the therapeutic needs of such children, and provide the requisite training for experienced caseworkers who wanted to treat them. A limited number of demonstration cases were conducted by Dr. Nagelberg, a clinical psychologist, under the principal author's supervision.

One of those cases was that of a boy, diagnosed as an early schizophrenic, and severely withdrawn. He is the subject of this case presentation.

In discussing the plan of treatment, it was hypothesized that Harry's basic problem was his vast reservoir of destructive im-pulsivity. Because of his inability to control its release and his oversensitivity to the pressures of the environment, he resorted to withdrawal to prevent himself from acting destructively.

responseSet.title: Early Thinking: The Training Process Develops
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Early Thinking: The Training Process Develops

Psychoanalysts have been complaining for years that the classroom does not contribute as much to the development of analysts as does personal analysis and supervision, that adequate training takes at least a decade, that candidates learn more through case supervision after graduation than before, and according to Price, (1988) that transference to an institute and its faculty may actually block learning.

While psychoanalysis itself has grown and changed, the teaching of children has also taken on new dimensions. Modern analysts felt that the method of training psychoanalysts could benefit from new concepts in childhood education. The founders of the modern analytic movement were practicing psychoanalysts trained, with one or two exceptions, by Hyman Spotnitz, a neurologist and psychiatrist who had been researching the treatment of schizophrenia and the other severe disorders.

In 1971, twenty analysts from the Theodor Reik Institute met to found a training center dedicated to these new principles of teaching; they scheduled a two-lecture series entitled “Techniques of Modern Psychoanalysis and Modern Psychoanalytic Theory” to introduce to the mental health community techniques for working with narcissistic patients. The lecturers were trained in modern analytic theory and had been teaching at psychoanalytic institutes, conducting workshops and courses at universities, and leading professional conferences on average for twenty years. The lecture series was a first step in the development of organized modern psychoanalytic teaching.

211

Epilogue

Hyman Spotnitz

Hyman Spotnitz

Hyman Spotnitz   Received his M.D. from Friedrich Wilhelms University in Berlin and his Med.Sc.D. in neurology from Physicians and Surgeons College, Columbia University. He is a Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association and the American Orthopsychiatric Association; Fellow of the American Group Psychotherapy Association. Currently in privatge practice of individual and group psychoanalytic psychotherapy in New York City, he has written and lectured extensively on analytic psychotherapy in the severe psychiatric disorders, analytic group psychotherapy and neurophysiology. In 1988, in recognition of his distinguished service to psychiatry and psychoanalytic research, he was presented with the Sigmund Freud Award of the American society of Psychoanalytic Physicians. His books include Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic Patient: Theory of the Technique, Psychotherapy of Preoedipal Conditions, The Couch and the Circle, and with Phyllis W. Meadow, Ph.D., Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses.

As the surviving member of the team that collaborated in the treatment of Harry Baker, I welcome the opportunity to reflect on the detailed report just presented. The fact that it is being published several decades after the case was conducted, in the nascent period of modern psychoanalysis, enables me to discuss it in the context of subsequent developments in the field.

Harry's therapist, Dr. T (as Leo Nagelberg is referred to in the case presentation) was greatly interested in understanding and learning how to treat severely disturbed youngsters under our borderline research and training project. I was equally interested in supervising him and other caseworkers who wanted to handle these difficult cases, and in training them in the use of techniques that I had found to be effective in my private psychoanalytic practice.

Before he met Harry, Dr. T was acquainted with my views on the basic problems and therapeutic needs of the children accepted for treatment under the project. He was initially instructed, for example, that they were hypersensitive to environmental pressures and terrified of losing control of themselves and behaving destructively. He was also instructed to try to behave somewhat like the patient to convey the message that nothing dangerously new would be injected into the relationship.

In the supervisory conferences on the case, held biweekly, Dr. T reported what had occurred since the preceding conference. After hearing his review of the material obtained from Harry and his own reactions to it, I functioned in the role of an accessory ego to increase his awareness of the totality of his emotional response to Harry and to help him deal with the problems that Harry presented.

[[RunningHead]]

The Clinical Program

Mental Hospital Placement Program Seminar and Clinical Psychoanalytic Psychopathology (PT 185)

The Center's program of clinical studies includes five years of direct work with patients.

Understanding preoedipal disorders, which are the conditions most challenging to contemporary analysts, is the goal of the first two years. During this time students are placed in a mental hospital where they are exposed to deeply regressed patients. A close study of these patients' preoccupations gives students an appreciation of the psychopathology continuum, from neurotic adjustment through character disorder, narcissism, somatization, and psychosis.

The fieldwork program was developed by Stanley Hayden, Genrald Fishbein, and myself to emphasize awareness of one's own primary process and its use working with severe pathologies. Stanley Hayden is the author of The toxic response in modern psychoanalysis and Some behavioral correlates of empathy. More recently Murray Sherman has been added to the fieldwork faculty. Dr. Sherman is co-author of Roles and Paradigms in Psychotherapy and author of Siding with the resistance in paradigmatic psychotherapy, Emotional communication in modern psychoanalysis, and numerous other articles. The fieldwork coordinator (originally Estelle Borowitz; now Rhoda Shapiro) interviews applicants for the program and assists them in arranging a two-year hospital placement. Shapiro has developed a mentor program permitting fieldwork students to elect to discuss their fieldwork concerns with a senior student.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Theory Sequence

The early Center program taught theory with the following emphases: basic psychoanalytic theory, early and late; modern psychoanalysis, introducing the concept of the narcissistic transference and its treatment; and the study of famous cases from the literature. After graduating three classes, we realized that our candidates were weak in the integration of technique with theory. We had developed many fine technicians, and those who were so inclined made up for deficiencies in Center requirements with self-directed reading. We realized that in order to develop future teachers and researchers, we needed to strengthen the Center's theoretical training. A modification of our open-admission policy was suggested, but, on review, we did not find that students from mental health disciplines were doing better than the others in developing themselves as therapeutic instruments. In fact, the unlearning required could, in some cases, be much more complicated where previous training had led to fixed ways of working with patients.

In a study of our student body completed in 1975, we discovered that approximately ten percent of the students came to the Center from the creative arts and other fields distinctly different in content from the mental health sciences. This study was done in preparation for the review of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis (NAAP) by the Office of Health, Education, and Welfare, for recognition of NAAP as an accrediting body. We were surprised to find that more research and writing were being done within this group than in our general student population.

313

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial Comment

Conforming to our policy of focusing from time to time on clinical material derived from an actual analytic relationship, we are pleased to devote this issue of the Journal to the report of a case that figured in the early history of modern psychoanalysis. This report is a session-by-session, annotated record of the treatment, during the 1950s, of a severely disturbed adolescent in a casework setting. The treatment was conducted under a research project directed by Hyman Spotnitz at a district office of the Jewish Board of Guardians, a New York City child guidance agency.

The treatment was conducted by the late Leo Nagelberg, a staff psychologist of the agency, under the supervision of Hyman Spotnitz. As supervisor of the JBG office where the boy met with Nagelberg over a period of four years, the late Yonata Feldman also functioned in a supervisory capacity. During her distinguished career in the training of social workers, Feldman remained active until shortly before her death in 1981. She conducted courses at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, helped to formulate its policies on supervision and training, and contributed articles to this Journal. One of her articles, “The Early History of Modern Psychoanalysis,” published in 1978, provides a fitting introduction to the case presentation that follows.

Development of the Narcissistic Transference

In Quest of a ‘Big Brother’

Harry Baker was 11 years old when his mother appealed to a child guidance agency for help in handling him. That first appeal did not lead to the opening of his case, however. In fact, the youngster was to observe two more birthdays before he acquired a case number and began building up a voluminous record of problems and progress.

In her first telephone call to the agency, his mother reported that Harry was losing interest in school. Up to then, his marks had been among the highest in his class. The boy was also becoming very depressed and irritable.

Mrs. Baker explained that she was a widow and spent a part of each day in her aged parents' home caring for them. Her daily absence from her own home greatly upset Harry, who told her that he'd rather be with her than play with other children. And, his mother had observed that the few children he did play with were younger than himself.

[Harry appeared to be withdrawing, to be losing contact with his peers, and reverting to the behavior of a much younger child. He seemed to be unwinding all his life ties except those binding him to his mother.]

Mrs. Baker was puzzled and worried. Could the agency assign one of its volunteer workers, one of the laymen who had come to be known as “Big Brothers,” to give her fatherless boy the male companionship and guidance he seemed to need?

Preface

June Bernstein

June Bernstein

June Bernstein  

When the Center opened its doors in 1971, it proposed to operate in accordance with two bold propositions: 1) that the resolution of resistance, a basic principle of psychoanalytic treatment, would be applied to the education of psychoanalytic candidates and, 2) that the psychoanalytic model including the couch can be used in the treatment of preverbal disorders. It was hypothesized that resistances to emotional learning were the greatest handicap to becoming a psychoanalyst. The method adopted by the Center and described herein was successful in helping students to develop tolerance for the feelings induced by patients and to increase their understanding of themselves. The Center has continued to develop its innovative approach to psychoanalytic education.

Phyllis Meadow, author of this issue devoted to the Center's teaching methods, is widely known for her energy and vision. A noted psychoanalytic educator, her published works indicate an abiding interest in how people learn and unlearn. As Dean of Curriculum at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, Meadow has the major responsibility of reviewing psychoanalytic literature and selecting readings for the modern analytic curriculum.

Her own classes are uniquely exciting—her keen interest in the subject being taught and the people learning it favors absorption of the material emotionally as well as intellectually. No student contact is dismissed or neglected in her classes. At the same time, the topic of the class, whether it be dreams, drives, or case management, is never lost sight of.

The History and Research Sequence

Unlike the maturation courses, history generates more interest in facts, and classes more closely resemble storytelling than process. This group consists of six courses on the history of psychoanalysis; two courses on psychoanalytic research constitute the balance of the history sequence.5 The material is organized around time periods in which events occurred or discoveries were made. The biographies of Freud, seven or more, if read independently, will assist students to feel comfortable with Freud, the man.

History of Psychoanalysis Prior to 1905 (PT 112)

This course traces the early developments in Freud's work, his method of analyzing data, and the effects of his friendships and career on his thinking. His Autobiographical note helps organize the influences on his early work; it traces his interest in hysteria to a trip to Paris and his work with Charcot. Career problems and the need for money in order to marry did not dampen his deep concern with the relationship between the nervous system and emotional functioning.
